chapters.title: Chapter 3: Cointegration — Testing Whether a Pair Really Mean-Reverts

lessons.title: The Engle-Granger Two-Step Method for Testing Cointegration

children.text: Lesson 10 gave you a tool to test whether one series is stationary. It said nothing about testing whether two price series, in levels, share a real long-run relationship. That is the actual cointegration question Lesson 9 raised, and answering it properly takes two coordinated steps, plus one adjustment that catches almost everyone the first time they try this.

body.text: The Engle-Granger method tests cointegration in two steps: regress one price series on the other to build the residual spread, exactly Lesson 6's hedge ratio construction, then test that residual for a unit root. The one adjustment: because the residual comes from an estimated regression rather than an observed series, it needs stricter critical values than Lesson 10's plain ADF table, not the same ones.

children.text: Step 1: Estimate the Hedge Ratio and Build the Residual

This step is nothing new. It is exactly Lesson 6's regression: fit Y = α + βX + ε by OLS on the two price series, and treat the residual, Y minus its predicted value, as the spread. What is new is what happens to that residual next.
Step 2: Test the Residual for a Unit Root, With the Right Critical Values

Run the same style of unit-root test from Lesson 10 on this residual series. If you reject the unit-root null, the residual is stationary, and the two price series are cointegrated using the β from Step 1 as the hedge ratio.

markDefs.definition: The bias introduced when a regression's fitted residual is tested as if it were an observed series, when in fact its coefficients were chosen specifically to minimize it, making it look artificially more stationary.

children.text: β in Step 1 was chosen specifically to make the residuals as small as possible, that is what OLS does by construction. This means the residual series is mechanically biased toward looking more well-behaved than a residual built from a truly unrelated pair would. Left uncorrected, this makes it too easy to falsely conclude two unrelated series are cointegrated. Statisticians call this the
, and the fix is to use stricter, more negative critical values, specifically derived for this two-step setup, rather than Lesson 10's plain ADF table.

body.caption: Plain ADF vs Engle-Granger cointegration critical values (illustrative, large-sample approximation, two-variable case)

body.text: A common mistake: building the residual exactly as in Lesson 6, running it through a plain adfuller() call, and comparing the result to Lesson 10's ADF critical value table. That comparison uses thresholds that are too lenient for this situation and can make an uncointegrated pair look cointegrated. Always use critical values meant for testing a regression residual, not an observed series.

children.text: In Practice: Use a Dedicated Cointegration Function
Rather than doing Step 1 and Step 2 by hand and looking up the adjusted critical values yourself, standard statistical libraries provide a single function that does both correctly.

body.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint

score, pvalue, critical_values = coint(hdfc_prices, icici_prices)

print("Test statistic:", round(score, 2))
print("p-value:", round(pvalue, 4))
print("Critical values (1%, 5%, 10%):", critical_values)
body.caption: statsmodels' coint() function runs both Engle-Granger steps internally and reports the correctly adjusted critical values

children.text: Worked Example: Two Pairs, Two Different Verdicts
Applying this to two pairs already discussed in this course produces two very different verdicts (illustrative results).

stats.label: HDFC Bank vs ICICI Bank: test statistic
stats.context: More negative than even the 1% Engle-Granger critical value of about −3.90

stats.label: HDFC Bank vs ICICI Bank: p-value
stats.context: Reject the null of no cointegration; the pair appears genuinely cointegrated

stats.label: Lesson 9's TCS/Infosys scenario: test statistic
stats.context: Far short of even the 10% critical value of about −3.05

stats.label: Lesson 9's TCS/Infosys scenario: p-value
stats.context: Fail to reject the null of no cointegration, consistent with the drifting price ratio Lesson 9 described

body.text: This closes the loop on Lesson 9's puzzle. The high, stable return correlation in that example was real, but the Engle-Granger test now confirms formally what the drifting price ratio chart already suggested: no cointegration. A high correlation reading and a failed cointegration test are not a contradiction, they are measuring two genuinely different things, exactly as Lesson 9 argued.

children.text: One More Caveat: Direction and Robustness

The Engle-Granger method is not perfectly symmetric. Regressing Y on X can give a slightly different residual, and occasionally a slightly different verdict in a finite sample, than regressing X on Y. Good practice is to check both directions and treat a result that only holds in one direction with some caution. For testing cointegration among more than two series at once, useful for basket trades beyond the scope of this course, the Johansen test is the standard multivariate extension, but the two-step Engle-Granger method covered here is the right tool for the pairs this course focuses on.

body.title: Why not just reuse Lesson 10's table?
body.question: You build a residual spread exactly as in Lesson 6, then run it through the plain ADF test from Lesson 10 and compare the statistic to Lesson 10's critical value table. What is wrong with this approach?
options: Nothing is wrong; the ADF test and its critical values work identically on any series
The residual was built using an estimated β that minimizes it, so it needs stricter, purpose-built cointegration critical values, not the plain ADF table
The ADF test cannot be run on residuals at all, only on raw price series
Lesson 10's critical values only apply to correlation, not to spreads
body.explanation: Because the hedge ratio β was estimated specifically to minimize the residual, the residual is mechanically biased toward looking more stationary than it would be for a genuinely unrelated pair. This generated regressor problem means the test needs the stricter, purpose-built Engle-Granger critical values, not Lesson 10's plain ADF table.

body.title: Which direction do you trust?
body.scenario: You test a candidate pair both ways. Regressing Nestle on Britannia and testing the residual rejects the null of no cointegration comfortably. Regressing Britannia on Nestle and testing that residual falls just short of rejecting at the 10% level.
body.prompt: What would you conclude, and what would you do next?
body.modelAnswer: This is exactly the kind of borderline, direction-sensitive result the Engle-Granger method can produce in finite samples. Rather than picking whichever direction supports the trade, you would treat this as weak, inconclusive evidence, extend the sample size if possible since a longer history reduces this sensitivity, and look for supporting economic reasoning, Lesson 4's kind of judgment, before treating the pair as a confirmed cointegrated candidate.

cards.definition: A procedure for testing whether two price series are cointegrated: first regress one on the other to build the residual spread, then test that residual for a unit root using critical values adjusted for the fact that it came from an estimated regression.

The bias introduced when a regression's fitted residual is tested as if it were an observed series, when in fact its coefficients were chosen specifically to minimize it, making it look artificially more stationary.
Stricter, more negative critical values, compared to plain ADF critical values, used specifically when testing a regression residual for cointegration, to correct for the generated regressor problem.

points: The Engle-Granger method has two steps: regress one price series on the other to build the residual spread (Lesson 6), then test that residual for a unit root.

Because the residual comes from an estimated regression, it needs stricter, purpose-built cointegration critical values, not Lesson 10's plain ADF table. Using the wrong table can make an uncointegrated pair look cointegrated.
Dedicated functions like statsmodels' coint() run both steps and apply the correct adjusted critical values automatically, which is safer than doing it by hand.
A pair can show high, stable correlation and still fail the Engle-Granger cointegration test, exactly the TCS/Infosys scenario from Lesson 9, now confirmed with a formal test.
The method is not perfectly symmetric; check both regression directions, and treat a result that only holds in one direction with caution rather than picking whichever supports the trade.
